items.title: Metric space: $d(x,y) = 0$ iff $x = y$, symmetry, and the triangle inequality; pseudometric and ultrametric

items.title: Cauchy sequence in a metric space

items.title: The extended real line $\overline{\mathbb{R}} = \mathbb{R} \cup \{-\infty, +\infty\}$, its order, and the arithmetic that is left undefined

Convergence in $\overline{\mathbb{R}}$ and the extended subsequential limit set: $L \in \overline{\mathbb{R}}$ is an extended subsequential limit when some subsequence converges to $L$, or diverges to $L = \pm\infty$
Limit superior and limit inferior of a real sequence as $\inf_n \sup_{k \ge n} x_k$ and $\sup_n \inf_{k \ge n} x_k$ in $\overline{\mathbb{R}}$
The tail suprema of any real sequence are nonincreasing in $\overline{\mathbb{R}}$, so the limit superior exists for every sequence
$\limsup(-x_k) = -\liminf(x_k)$, with the reflection of $\overline{\mathbb{R}}$ exchanging $\pm\infty$
$\liminf x_k \le \limsup x_k$ for every real sequence
For finite $L$: $L = \limsup x_k$ iff for every $\varepsilon > 0$ one has $x_k < L + \varepsilon$ eventually and $x_k > L - \varepsilon$ frequently
A real sequence converges to $L \in \mathbb{R}$ iff $\liminf x_k = \limsup x_k = L$, and diverges to $\pm\infty$ iff both equal $\pm\infty$
The limit superior is itself a subsequential limit in $\overline{\mathbb{R}}$ and is the greatest one
The limit inferior is the least subsequential limit in $\overline{\mathbb{R}}$
If each $y_j$ is a subsequential limit of $(x_k)$ and $y_j \to y \in \mathbb{R}$, then $y$ is a subsequential limit of $(x_k)$
If $x_k \le y_k$ eventually then $\limsup x_k \le \limsup y_k$ and $\liminf x_k \le \liminf y_k$
$\limsup(x_k + y_k) \le \limsup x_k + \limsup y_k$ whenever the right-hand side is defined in $\overline{\mathbb{R}}$, and dually for $\liminf$
For bounded nonnegative sequences, $\limsup(x_k y_k) \le (\limsup x_k)(\limsup y_k)$
For every $a > 0$, $a^{1/n} \to 1$
For $a_k > 0$: $\liminf a_{k+1}/a_k \le \liminf a_k^{1/k} \le \limsup a_k^{1/k} \le \limsup a_{k+1}/a_k$
For every $p > 0$ and every positive rational $\alpha$, $n^{\alpha}/(1+p)^n \to 0$
For every real $x$, $x^k/k! \to 0$

items.title: The five completeness properties of an ordered field: least upper bound, monotone convergence, nested intervals, Bolzano-Weierstrass, and Cauchy completeness

items.title: Series, partial sums, convergence and the sum, divergence, and the tail series
A series converges iff each of its tail series converges, and the sum splits as $s_N$ plus the $N$-th tail
If a series converges then its terms tend to $0$
A series converges iff for every $\varepsilon > 0$ there is $N$ with $|a_{m+1} + \dots + a_n| < \varepsilon$ for all $n > m \ge N$
Convergent series add and scale termwise
For $|r| < 1$, $\sum_{k \ge 0} r^k = 1/(1-r)$, and for $|r| \ge 1$ the series diverges
$\sum (b_k - b_{k+1})$ converges iff $(b_k)$ converges, with sum $b_0 - \lim b_k$
A series of nonnegative terms converges iff its partial sums are bounded, and then the sum is their supremum
If $0 \le a_k \le b_k$ eventually, convergence of $\sum b_k$ gives convergence of $\sum a_k$, and divergence of $\sum a_k$ gives divergence of $\sum b_k$

Whenever the ratio test decides, the root test decides the same way, and the converse fails
Kummer: with $\zeta_k > 0$, $\liminf(\zeta_k a_k/a_{k+1} - \zeta_{k+1}) > 0$ gives convergence, and if $\sum 1/\zeta_k$ diverges while that expression is eventually $\le 0$ the series diverges

Raabe is Kummer with $\zeta_k = k+1$: $\liminf\, (k+1)(a_k/a_{k+1} - 1) > 1$ gives convergence and $\limsup < 1$ gives divergence
Gauss: if $a_k/a_{k+1} = 1 + h/k + r_k$ with $|r_k| \le C\,k^{-1-\varepsilon}$ for $k \ge 1$, some constant $C$ and some rational $\varepsilon > 0$, the series converges iff $h > 1$

Basis and subbasis for a topology, and the topology generated by a family of sets

A family is a basis for a unique topology iff it covers the set and every point of an intersection of two members lies in a member inside that intersection; finite intersections of any subbasis form a basis

Interior, closure, boundary, exterior, derived set and isolated point in a topological space
A point lies in the closure of $A$ iff every basic neighbourhood of it meets $A$; the closure is the smallest closed superset and equals $A$ together with its derived set

Interior commutes with finite intersections and closure with finite unions, while the two reverse combinations are inclusions only and both fail for infinite families; the space is the disjoint union of interior, boundary and exterior
